aliases.name: Coiste Bodhar
aliases.meaning: deaf or silent coach (the death coach)

description.summary: A headless rider of Irish folklore who appears as a harbinger of death, riding a black horse and carrying his own severed head.
description.full: The Dullahan is a figure from Irish folklore — a member of the Unseelie host described as a headless rider who carries his severed head with him. He travels alone or driving a black coach (the Coiste Bodhar) drawn by six black horses, and stops only at the home of someone about to die. When he speaks, only one word is uttered: the name of the person whose soul is being summoned. Documented in detail in 19th-century Irish folklore collections, especially Thomas Crofton Croker's Fairy Legends and Traditions of the South of Ireland (1825–1828) and W. B. Yeats's Fairy and Folk Tales of the Irish Peasantry (1888), the Dullahan is closely linked to the wider European 'wild hunt' and headless-horseman traditions and is widely cited as an inspiration for Washington Irving's Headless Horseman in 'The Legend of Sleepy Hollow' (1820).

etymology.origin: Anglicization of Irish 'dubhlachán' or 'dulachán', from 'dubh' (black, dark) plus a diminutive ending; also linked by some glossaries to 'dorr/durr' (anger) or 'durrach' (malicious, fierce).
etymology.meaning: 'Dark man' or 'gloomy little fellow'; also rendered as 'without a head' (Gan Ceann).
etymology.first_use: Recorded in English-language print in the 19th century; Croker's 1825–1828 collection is the earliest widely cited.

features.description: The Dullahan's head, removed from the body, is carried under the arm or held aloft; it is described by Croker as resembling a stale cheese with depressed features and enormous eyes that dart about
Rides a black horse, or drives the Coiste Bodhar (death coach) drawn by six black horses
Carries a whip said to be made from a human spinal column

features.feature: Gates and locks open of their own accord
features.description: All gates, doors, and locks open before him, regardless of fastenings

features.feature: Silent except to name the dying
features.description: Utters only the name of the person about to die; otherwise silent

physical.morphology: Anthropomorphic male rider of human size, decapitated; the carried head is presented as alive and observant despite being detached.

abilities.description: Calls aloud the name of the person whose soul is to be taken, sealing their death
Locked gates, walls, and doors yield in his presence
May throw a basin of blood in the face of anyone who watches him pass; that person is marked for death or struck blind in one eye
The only known protection: even a small amount of gold reportedly causes the Dullahan to vanish

behavior.diet: Not described; the Dullahan is an undead messenger rather than a corporeal feeder
patterns: Rides at night, particularly on Irish feast days such as Samhain
Stops outside the home of a person about to die and calls their name
Disappears at dawn or when confronted with gold
Does not respond to questioning; cannot be detained

range.description: Folkloric range across the island of Ireland, with the densest narrative tradition in the southern counties documented by Crofton Croker and the western counties documented by Yeats and later folklorists.

hotspots.name: County Sligo

location.description: Rural County Sligo, especially the area around Sligo town and Drumcliff

hotspots.notes: Region from which W. B. Yeats collected and published Dullahan tales

hotspots.name: County Cork

first_recorded.source: Crofton Croker, 'Fairy Legends and Traditions of the South of Ireland' (1825–1828)

peak_activity_periods.description: Documentation peak during the Irish folklore revival

temporal.seasonal_patterns: Strongly associated with Samhain (1 November) and other Irish feast days when the boundary between worlds is held to be thin.

origins.cultural_roots: Irish (Gaelic) folk tradition; identified by 19th-century folklorists as one of the solitary fairies of the Unseelie court.
origins.earliest_accounts: Earliest written accounts in English appear in Thomas Crofton Croker's three-volume 'Fairy Legends and Traditions of the South of Ireland' (1825–1828).
origins.folklore_connections: Connected to a wider European tradition of headless riders (German Wütende Heer, Scandinavian Aaskereia), Breton Ankou, and English/Continental Wild Hunt; influenced Washington Irving's Headless Horseman.

timeline.event: Thomas Crofton Croker publishes the first volume of 'Fairy Legends and Traditions of the South of Ireland', containing detailed Dullahan and Coiste Bodhar accounts
timeline.significance: First English-language print documentation of the Dullahan

timeline.event: W. B. Yeats publishes 'Fairy and Folk Tales of the Irish Peasantry', collecting and reframing earlier Dullahan accounts
timeline.significance: Anchors the Dullahan in the Irish Literary Revival canon

timeline.event: Folklorist Patricia Lysaght and others begin systematic academic study of Irish death-messenger figures
timeline.significance: Modern folkloristics frames the Dullahan alongside the banshee in death-omen tradition

history.modern_era: The Dullahan persists as a stock figure of Irish heritage media, Halloween folklore, and dark fantasy. Patricia Lysaght's scholarship on Irish death-messengers and the Dúchas digital archive of the Irish National Folklore Collection have made primary-source Dullahan testimonies more publicly available.

documentary.name: Croker's 'Fairy Legends and Traditions of the South of Ireland'
documentary.description: Three-volume folklore collection containing the foundational English-language Dullahan and Coiste Bodhar narratives, including 'The Good Woman' and 'Hanlon's Mill'.
documentary.analysis: Acknowledged as the principal documentary source for the Dullahan in scholarly folkloristics; presented as folktale, not eyewitness report.

documentary.name: Yeats's 'Fairy and Folk Tales of the Irish Peasantry'
documentary.description: Anthology that re-presents earlier Dullahan accounts and includes the figure under the rubric of solitary fairies.
documentary.analysis: Editorial reworking of earlier 19th-century field collections.

paranormal.name: Death messenger of the Otherworld
paranormal.description: The Dullahan is a member of the Unseelie / Sluagh, dispatched from the Otherworld to summon the dying.

skeptical.name: Folkloric narrative without referent
skeptical.description: The Dullahan is a literary-folkloric figure without an extant phenomenological basis; its 'sightings' are stories rather than encounter reports.
evidence_cited: Pattern follows European headless-rider archetype rather than localized phenomenology

skeptical.name: Diffusion from European headless-rider archetype
skeptical.description: The Dullahan represents the Irish localization of a wider European headless-horseman / Wild Hunt narrative complex.
evidence_cited: Parallels with Ankou, Wütende Heer, and Aaskereia traditions
Late date of first textual attestation

folklore.beliefs: The Dullahan's calling of a name was held to be inevitable and unappealable; the only known protection was gold, even in trace amount. Watching him pass risked having a basin of blood thrown in one's face or being struck blind in one eye.
